title: Zara and the Tide Secret
markdown:
Pebble Beach Harbour smelled of salt and wet rope. Tiny boats bobbed at their posts like cheerful corks, except today they were not bobbing so much as sitting, keels kissing mud. The science club had come for a race. The sea had come for a sulk.

Zara, who missed very little with her nature-finder’s eyes, stood on barnacle rock and measured the gap between hope and water. It was a large gap.

“It’s too low,” Leo grumbled, and scraped his knee, which did not raise the harbour. “We can’t get the keels in without bumping.”

Maria’s pigtails flopped. They tried pushing. They tried pulling. Faces went pink. Driftwood sticks helped not at all. The sea sat, stubbornly shallow, as if it had not been invited.

“It’s like the sea is playing hide-and-seek,” Zara said, quieter than she meant. The race was supposed to start now. They were surrounded by water they could not use.

A flash of glossy black, a clatter of something shiny. Cora the jackdaw landed on a post that was usually a drowned thing and today was a perch. Cora collected sparkle: buttons, sea glass, foil. She had been watching the hullabaloo with the professional interest of a bird who knows that humans drop treasure when they flap.

She tilted her head. Sky. Water. Sky again. Then she hopped to the water’s edge, picked up a smooth grey pebble, and flew to a higher stretch of wall. Plink. The pebble went in. The water did not leap up to meet it. She tried another. Still nothing.

Zara stopped shoving boats. Cora was not filling the harbour. Cora was looking.

The jackdaw left the pebble on a wet line of weed, a little marker, then went back to preening as if she had not done anything clever. Time passed in gull-cries and the slap of empty hulls. When Zara looked again, the weed-line pebble was under water. The post Cora had used as a dry seat had a wet sock of sea around it.

Cora cawed, hopped to a new edge, and set another pebble. She was following the water, not arguing with it.

Zara felt the click that is not quite a sound. Teacher Lin had spoken in class of the moon and the oceans, not as poetry, as a pull. Zara looked up. The moon was a pale coin, visible even in the washing daylight, hanging as if it had every right to be there.

She did not announce that a plump moon made a high sea and a sliver made a puddle. That would have been tidy and wrong. She watched Cora’s markers drown, one after another, and remembered the invisible string.

“The moon,” she said, and her voice found its volume. “It’s pulling the water.”

Leo squinted upward. Maria stopped frowning at her shoes.

“When the water is high, that’s high tide. We can launch. When it’s crawled away, that’s low tide. That’s now. Or it was now. Look — Cora’s first pebble is swimming.”

She pointed at the darkening sky as evening leaned in. “The moon’s gravity tugs the Earth’s water. It makes the sea bulge toward it, and another bulge on the far side. High tide twice a day. Low tide twice a day. We were trying to race at the empty hour.”

Cora let out a caw that had no need of a translation.

“So,” Leo said slowly, “if we watch the water — and the moon — we’ll know when it’s high enough?”

“We wait,” Zara said, and the worry of speaking up went out like a wet match. “We plan races for high tide. Cora already was.”

Teacher Lin, who had been on the wall with a proud quiet, clapped once, softly. “The moon’s pull moves the oceans. You’ve caught it doing so, Zara. Not in a book. In a harbour that would not float a keel until it was ready.”

The water kept coming, unembarrassed. Keels found it. Leo forgot his knee. Maria’s pigtails bounced for a better reason. Cora stole a bottle cap and considered it a prize equal to science.

Zara watched the posts put on their wet socks and thought of the next low, which would come whether they had a race or not. She would bring a pebble of her own next time, to mark the line, and see how far the moon’s string could tug before it let go.
characters: Zara (trail naturalist), Cora (jackdaw), Teacher Lin (teacher), Leo (clubmate), Maria (clubmate)
